posts.title: Automatic night light
posts.description: A light-dependent resistor watches the room and a lamp comes on when it gets dark. Drag the LDR's light level down in the inspector and watch it switch. The threshold is one number at the top of the sketch.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: The lamp follows the dark
tests.description: Daylight leaves it off; dimming the LDR turns it on.

posts.title: Plant thirst alarm
posts.description: A soil probe in the pot and a buzzer that chirps when it dries out. These probes read HIGH when dry, which catches everyone out once — set the moisture low in the inspector to hear it.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: It chirps only when dry
tests.description: Damp soil is quiet; dry soil chirps and says so.

posts.title: Reaction timer
posts.description: The LED lights, you hit the button, the sketch tells you how long you took. millis() and a busy-wait — about the smallest game there is. Press the button on the canvas when the LED comes on.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: A press is timed
tests.description: The LED lights after a second, and a press is reported in milliseconds.

posts.title: Fever check thermometer
posts.description: An LM35 and two LEDs: green under 37.5 °C, red at or above. The conversion is the LM35's 10 mV per degree and nothing else. Set the temperature in the inspector — try 39.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: Red means fever
tests.description: Room temperature lights green; 39 °C lights red.

posts.title: Motion-activated porch light
posts.description: A PIR sensor and a light that stays on for five seconds after the last movement, timed with millis() so the sketch never blocks. Tick "Motion detected" in the inspector to walk past it.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

posts.title: Parking distance beeper
posts.description: An HC-SR04 on the garage wall: the closer the car, the faster it beeps, solid under 15 cm. Distance comes from timing the echo pulse, exactly as on the bench. Drag the distance slider to park.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: Close means beeping
tests.description: At 40 cm it beeps; the distance is reported.

posts.title: Desk climate monitor
posts.description: A BMP280 read with raw Wire calls and the datasheet's own compensation, no library, and three LEDs for too cold, comfortable and too warm. Set the sensor's temperature in the inspector and the right LED lights. A good first look at what a sensor library is doing for you.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: Comfortable, then too warm
tests.description: The default 25 °C is comfortable; 30 °C lights the warm LED.

posts.title: Five-LED bubble level
posts.description: An MPU6050 as a spirit level: pitch from the accelerometer with the usual atan2, shown as a "bubble" that slides along five LEDs. Tilt it with the Pitch slider in the inspector. Raw registers, no library — waking the chip is one write to 0x6B.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: Level, then tilted
tests.description: Flat lights the middle LED; 30° forward slides the bubble to the end.

posts.title: Pico pedestrian crossing
posts.description: Traffic lights on a Raspberry Pi Pico with a crossing button: green until someone presses, then amber, then red while it says WALK. A small state machine with no delay() in the button path, so a press is never missed. Output on Serial1, the UART the emulator runs.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: A press stops the traffic
tests.description: Green until the button, then amber, then red with WALK.

posts.title: 4-bit computer built from logic chips
posts.description: A real accumulator machine on the bench: a 74HC161 program counter, a 74HC157 to choose LOAD or ADD, a 74HC283 adder, a 74HC574 accumulator with a carry flag, and a CD4511 driving the display. The Uno is only the program memory — it puts each instruction on the bus and pulses the clock, then reads back what the chips computed. Watch the program counter count, the accumulator reach 9, and the carry flag light when it overflows. Change the ROM table to write your own program.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: The chips compute 3 x 3, then overflow
tests.description: Every value is read back off the accumulator's pins: the Uno only supplies the program.

posts.title: Snake on an 8×8 LED matrix
posts.description: The whole game on a MAX7219 matrix: an analog joystick steers, the snake grows when it eats, a buzzer clicks on every bite and sounds when you crash. The matrix driver is programmed register by register over hardware SPI — no library — so every pixel you see is a byte the sketch sent. Drag the joystick in the inspector (or click it on the canvas) to play.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: Eat, turn, crash
tests.description: The first bite is straight ahead; pushing the stick up turns the snake into the top wall.

posts.title: Keypad combination safe
posts.description: A 4×4 keypad scanned by hand, a servo as the bolt, a 16×2 LCD on an I2C backpack driven straight from the HD44780 datasheet, and LEDs and a buzzer for right and wrong. Type 1234 then # on the keypad — click the keys on the canvas — and the bolt swings open for three seconds. Get it wrong and it tells you.

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: A wrong code, then the right one
tests.description: Typed on the keypad matrix itself: 9 # is refused, 1 2 3 4 # opens the bolt.

posts.title: Four-chip weather station on one I2C bus
posts.description: A BMP280, an SHT31, a DS3231 clock and a 20×4 LCD sharing two wires, every byte sent by hand: the BMP280's full temperature and pressure compensation from the datasheet, the SHT31's single-shot measurement, BCD time from the RTC, and the LCD in 4-bit mode behind its PCF8574. Set the temperature, pressure or humidity on any sensor in the inspector; push the humidity past 70% and the alarm goes off.

project.name: Four-chip weather station on one I2C bus

codeFiles.name: sketch.ino

tests.name: Every sensor answers, and humidity raises the alarm
tests.description: Readings come off the bus with the datasheet arithmetic; 82% humidity lights the amber LED.

posts.title: Two boards, one bus: Pico to Uno
posts.description: Two microcontrollers, each running its own sketch in its own emulator, joined by nothing but wires: the Pico reads a DIP switch and sends the value over a 4-bit parallel bus with a strobe line, and the Uno latches it on the strobe and drives a seven-segment display through a CD4511. Flip the switches on the canvas and the digit changes on the other board. Each board has its own sketch tab.

project.name: Two boards, one bus: Pico to Uno

uno_receiver.ino

tests.description: Switches 1 and 3 on make 5, strobed out on GP14. (The bench runs the Pico; both boards run together live.)
